title: What is the difference between `COPY` and `ADD` in a Dockerfile, and why is `COPY` usually preferred?
shortTitle: COPY Versus ADD in a Dockerfile and Why COPY Is Usually Preferred

s1_definition.profdef: `COPY` and `ADD` both copy files from the build context into the image, but `ADD` has two extra behaviours: it can fetch a file from a remote URL, and it automatically extracts a local compressed archive (such as a `.tar.gz`) into the destination. `COPY` does neither; it simply copies local files and directories exactly as they are. `COPY` is usually preferred because it is explicit and predictable: it does exactly one thing, so there are no surprises like unexpected auto-extraction or pulling an unverified file over the network. `ADD` is reserved for the specific cases where its auto-extraction is genuinely wanted; remote downloads are better done with an explicit, verifiable tool.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of two mailroom clerks at the National Bank of India. `COPY` is the careful clerk who takes exactly the documents you hand him and places them on the desk, unchanged, every time. `ADD` is an over-eager clerk who, if you hand him a sealed box, might decide to open it and spread its contents across the desk (auto-extracting an archive), and if you give him an address he might go out and fetch a parcel from an unknown sender (downloading from a URL). For a bank that values predictability and security, you want the careful clerk by default, and you only ask the eager clerk to open a box when that is specifically what you need.
s1_definition.oneliner: COPY copies local files exactly as-is, ADD additionally auto-extracts archives and can fetch URLs, so prefer COPY for predictability and security and use ADD only when you actually want archive extraction.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `COPY` and `ADD` both copy files from the build context into the image, but `ADD` has two extra behaviours: it can fetch a file from a remote URL, and it automatically extracts a local compressed archive (such as a `.tar.gz`) into the destination. `COPY` does neither; it simply copies local files and directories exactly as they are. `COPY` is usually preferred because it is explicit and predictable: it does exactly one thing, so there are no surprises like unexpected auto-extraction or pulling an unverified file over the network. `ADD` is reserved for the specific cases where its auto-extraction is genuinely wanted; remote downloads are better done with an explicit, verifiable tool.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of two mailroom clerks at the National Bank of India. `COPY` is the careful clerk who takes exactly the documents you hand him and places them on the desk, unchanged, every time. `ADD` is an over-eager clerk who, if you hand him a sealed box, might decide to open it and spread its contents across the desk (auto-extracting an archive), and if you give him an address he might go out and fetch a parcel from an unknown sender (downloading from a URL). For a bank that values predictability and security, you want the careful clerk by default, and you only ask the eager clerk to open a box when that is specifically what you need.

**One line to remember:** COPY copies local files exactly as-is, ADD additionally auto-extracts archives and can fetch URLs, so prefer COPY for predictability and security and use ADD only when you actually want archive extraction.

sections.s2_technical:
Both instructions share the same basic job and syntax: they take a source from the build context and a destination path inside the image, for example `COPY target/app.jar /app/app.jar` or `ADD target/app.jar /app/app.jar`. For a plain local file, the two behave identically.

The first difference is archive auto-extraction. If the source is a recognised local compressed archive, `ADD` automatically unpacks it into the destination directory. So `ADD release.tar.gz /app/` expands the tarball's contents into `/app/`, whereas `COPY release.tar.gz /app/` places the tarball file itself into `/app/` without unpacking. This auto-extraction is occasionally convenient but often surprising, because a reader of the Dockerfile cannot tell from the line alone whether a file or an unpacked tree ends up in the image.

The second difference is remote URL fetching. `ADD https://example.com/file.jar /app/` downloads the file over the network into the image. `COPY` cannot do this. Relying on `ADD` for downloads is discouraged because the download is not cached well, you cannot easily verify a checksum or signature inline, and it bakes an external network dependency and a potentially unverified file into your build, which is a supply-chain risk.

This is why `COPY` is preferred as the default. It does exactly one predictable thing, so Dockerfiles are easier to read and reason about, and there is no risk of accidental extraction or of silently pulling an unexpected remote file. The official Docker best practices explicitly recommend `COPY` unless you specifically need `ADD`'s auto-extraction of a local archive.

When `ADD` is the right choice, it is narrow: you have a local archive that you deliberately want extracted into the image in one step, and you accept that behaviour explicitly. For remote files, the recommended pattern is to download with an explicit tool in a `RUN` step where you can verify a checksum, for example running a curl or wget followed by a `sha256sum -c` check, which makes the provenance auditable.

A senior nuance is the supply-chain and security angle, which matters a lot in banking. `ADD` from a URL fetches a file you have not verified and cannot easily pin, so a compromised or changed remote could silently alter your image; an explicit download with checksum verification in a `RUN` step closes that gap. Another nuance is caching and reproducibility: `COPY` of local files participates cleanly in layer caching, while `ADD` from a URL can behave unpredictably across builds. A third nuance is readability as a form of safety: in a reviewed banking Dockerfile, every line should do an obvious thing, and `COPY` honours that, whereas `ADD` hides whether extraction happens, so defaulting to `COPY` makes reviews and audits more reliable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A Dockerfile for the transfer service used `ADD config-bundle.tar.gz /app/config/` expecting the file to be placed there, but `ADD` silently extracted it, scattering dozens of files into the image and breaking the expected path. Nobody could tell from the line what had happened. This is exactly the predictability problem `COPY` solves. `COPY` would have placed the archive exactly as given, and if extraction was wanted it would be an explicit, visible step.

Problem 2 — Another Dockerfile used `ADD https://some-mirror/driver.jar /app/libs/` to pull a database driver, with no checksum. A mirror change once served a different file, and the image shipped an unverified driver into a banking service. This is exactly the supply-chain problem that avoiding `ADD`-from-URL solves. An explicit download with a verified checksum in a `RUN` step makes the provenance auditable.

Problem 3 — Code reviewers kept missing subtle behaviour differences between the two instructions. This is exactly the readability-as-safety problem that defaulting to `COPY` solves. Every `COPY` line does one obvious thing, so reviews are reliable.

To make this concrete we will write a Java simulation that models how `COPY` and `ADD` differ. We will model a `FileCopier` (COPY) that places a source exactly as-is, and an `AddCopier` (ADD) that auto-extracts recognised archives and can fetch a URL. We will run both against a plain JAR (identical result), against a tarball (COPY keeps it, ADD extracts it), and against a URL (COPY refuses, ADD fetches an unverified file). We will also show the preferred verified-download pattern. This mirrors the real behavioural and security differences.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.copyadd.CopyVsAddDemo

# Real usage: prefer COPY; verify remote downloads
docker build -f Dockerfile.copy-preferred -t transfer-service:1.2.0 .
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is three sources: a plain JAR, a local tarball config bundle, and a remote URL for a database driver.

Step 1: For the plain JAR, COPY places it exactly at /app/ and ADD does the same. For a simple local file the two are identical, which is why many Dockerfiles use them interchangeably without noticing a difference.

Step 2: For the config tarball, COPY places the archive file itself into /app/config/, so the image filesystem contains the tarball unchanged. The result is predictable: what you named is what is there.

Step 3: For the same tarball, ADD auto-extracts it, so the image filesystem contains the unpacked contents under an extracted directory rather than the archive. The log warns that this extraction is not obvious from the line, which is exactly the surprise that breaks expectations.

Step 4: For the remote URL, COPY refuses because it cannot fetch URLs, and logs that a verified RUN download should be used instead. This is the safe behaviour: no silent network fetch.

Step 5: For the same URL, ADD fetches the file, and because it is unverified the log flags a supply-chain risk, since a changed or compromised remote could ship a different file into the banking image. The demo closes by stating the preferred pattern: COPY for local files, and an explicit, checksum-verified RUN download for remote files.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Source
    │
    ├─ PLAIN FILE
    │    COPY → /app/file (as-is)      ADD → /app/file (same)
    │
    ├─ LOCAL ARCHIVE (.tar.gz)
    │    COPY → /app/archive.tar.gz    ADD → /app/extracted/* (AUTO-EXTRACT!)

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
COPY and ADD both copy files from the build context into the image, and for a plain local file they behave identically. The difference is that ADD has two extra behaviours that COPY does not. First, ADD automatically extracts a recognised local compressed archive into the destination, so ADD of a tar.gz unpacks its contents, whereas COPY of the same file just places the archive as-is. Second, ADD can fetch a file from a remote URL into the image, which COPY cannot do at all.

COPY is preferred as the default precisely because it does exactly one predictable thing. A reader of the Dockerfile can tell from a COPY line exactly what ends up in the image, with no risk of accidental extraction and no silent network fetch. ADD hides whether extraction happens, so the same-looking line can place either a file or an unpacked tree, which is a readability and correctness hazard. The official Docker best practices recommend COPY unless you specifically need ADD's local-archive extraction.

The security angle is what makes me strict about this in banking. ADD from a URL fetches a file I have not verified and cannot easily pin, so a changed or compromised remote could silently alter the image, which is a supply-chain risk. The correct pattern for a remote file is to download it explicitly in a RUN step and verify its checksum right there, so the provenance is auditable. ADD is justified only in the narrow case of deliberately extracting a local archive in one step, where I accept that behaviour explicitly.

On the banking project this came up twice. One Dockerfile used ADD on a config tarball expecting the file to be placed, but it silently extracted and scattered files, breaking the expected path, and switching to COPY made it predictable. Another used ADD from a mirror URL with no checksum, and when the mirror changed, the service shipped an unverified driver; we replaced that with a COPY-based image plus an explicit curl-and-sha256sum verification in a RUN step. The senior point I always add is that I treat COPY as the default across the board, use a linter like hadolint to flag ADD-from-URL in reviews, and reserve ADD strictly for intended local-archive extraction, because in a reviewed banking Dockerfile every line should do one obvious, verifiable thing.
